title: SMTP-DANE (RFC 7672): dedicated entry point, not a reuse of the HTTPS DANE path
description:
## Why

RFC 7672 SMTP-DANE has the strongest production deployment of any DANE flavour — MTAs negotiating TLS routinely use it for trust. A workspace that adopts DANE for HTTPS and not SMTP is incomplete. Replaces PKIX-j32w.6, which asked the question against a function (verify_smtp_signer) that does not exist and would have been the wrong home anyway: SMTP-DANE validates a mail SERVER's TLS certificate, not a signer.

## Why this cannot reuse verify_tls_server's DANE path

Three behavioural differences from HTTPS-DANE. The first makes a shared path wrong rather than merely incomplete.

### 1. Usage filtering — CONFIRM THIS FIRST

Current understanding is that RFC 7672 requires SMTP clients to ignore PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1) records outright, because public CA trust is not meaningful between MTAs with no user to see a warning: only DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) apply.

THIS IS NOT CONFIRMED. Read RFC 7672 §3.1 and the surrounding text before writing any code. If it holds, then a shared code path with verify_tls_server would honour usage-0 and usage-1 records that SMTP-DANE requires be ignored — a silent policy violation, and the reason this needs its own entry point. If it does not hold, re-evaluate whether a shared path with a mode flag is adequate after all.

### 2. DNSSEC-validated MX lookup — reaches into the resolver

The TLSA owner name derives from an MX lookup, and that lookup must itself be DNSSEC-validated. An unvalidated MX lookup lets an attacker rewrite the MX record and point the connection at a server whose TLSA record they also control, which defeats the whole mechanism.

This is a pkix-dane-resolver requirement, not a wrapper concern: it needs a validated multi-step lookup (MX, then TLSA under the resulting hostname), with the DNSSEC status of BOTH steps surfaced. pkix-dane's TlsaResolver trait as shipped resolves a single TlsaName and has no MX concept. Expect either an additional trait method or a sibling trait in pkix-dane-resolver. Check whether this changes what PKIX-j32w.2 should build before that bead starts.

### 3. Reference identity

Which name the certificate must match follows RFC 7672's MX-derived rules rather than RFC 6125 hostname matching. Determine how this composes with pkix-identity rather than reimplementing name matching.

## Placement — open

PKIX-j32w.6 left this open: pkix-chain wrapper, or a sibling pkix-smtp crate. Decide once the resolver-side shape from difference 2 is known, since an MX-aware resolver trait may make a sibling crate the natural home.

## Also in scope

- RFC 7672's own opportunistic-vs-mandatory posture at the SMTP level, and how it composes with the DaneFailurePolicy decided in PKIX-j32w.4. These are different layers and may not agree; work out which wins.
- Whether the dane / dane-resolver feature split decided on PKIX-j32w.3 extends here unchanged.

## Depends on

pkix-dane 0.2.0 (shipped). Resolver work is PKIX-j32w.2; this bead should be read before that one starts, because difference 2 may widen its scope.

## Acceptance

[ ] RFC 7672 usage-filtering requirement confirmed against the RFC text and recorded
[ ] MX lookup is DNSSEC-validated, with the status of both lookup steps surfaced to the caller
[ ] Usage 0 and 1 records handled per the confirmed RFC requirement
[ ] Reference identity follows RFC 7672, composed with pkix-identity rather than reimplemented
[ ] Placement decided and recorded
notes:
PIECES A AND B DONE 2026-11-24. Piece C (the entry point) remains, plus the DaneFailurePolicy reconciliation.

## Done

A. §3.2 name checks
   - pkix_identity::verify_dns_name_with_cn_fallback -- §3.2.3 matching (14 tests)
   - pkix_dane::smtp -- SmtpIdentities (the §3.2.2 identifier set), verify_smtp_name (18 tests)

B. §2.1 / §2.2 discovery
   - pkix_dane::smtp_lookup -- MxResolution sans-IO state machine, MxStep/MxAnswer, DeliveryTarget, SmtpDaneConfig, resolve_with (22 tests)

Both behind the `smtp` feature. Builds for thumbv7em-none-eabi. 2012 workspace tests pass.

## The two MUSTs, implemented and mutation-tested

MX PREFERENCE OUTRANKS CHANNEL SECURITY (§2.2.1). A worse-preference host with TLSA records MUST NOT preempt a better-preference host without them. Preferring the DANE-capable host is a conformance bug and the obvious thing to write. Test: backup MX has the TLSA records, primary has none, primary must still be offered first without DANE.

Verified the test is not vacuous by reversing the sort in the implementation -- it fails that test plus two others, and passes again on restore. Worth doing for any test whose whole value is catching an inversion.

ADDRESS LOOKUPS PRECEDE TLSA LOOKUPS (§2.2.2). With an insecure address answer, the TLSA query is not issued AT ALL. That is the half that matters: broken load-balancing nameservers at some large providers answer TLSA with SERVFAIL or NOTIMP instead of an insecure negative reply, and a query never sent cannot strand the message.

## Design notes worth keeping

Sans-IO was the right call and cheaper than expected. The lookup decisions are pure functions of DNS answers, so no resolver is needed to test the surprising rules -- each test scripts the answers directly. The resolver side becomes a thin driver.

RrsetTrust collapses Indeterminate into Insecure AT THE BOUNDARY rather than at each decision site. §2.1.1 requires it and "All 'insecure' RRsets MUST be handled identically"; collapsing once means no later code has to remember.

An insecure CNAME leading to a signed MX RRset still counts as insecure. §2.2.1 says "the MX RRset (or any CNAME leading to it)". A "last answer wins" implementation misses this; the state machine only ever weakens mx_secure, never strengthens it.

A failed TLSA lookup disqualifies a reachable server -- the only place in this profile where that happens. Failing open would let anyone able to drop TLSA responses downgrade every connection.

Equal MX preferences keep input order, deliberately: the machine stays deterministic and testable, RFC 5321 §5.1 randomization is the caller's to apply by shuffling first, and §2.2.1 explicitly does not oblige an MTA to prefer the more secure of two equal-preference hosts.

## Piece C: what remains

1. THE DaneFailurePolicy RECONCILIATION, which is the substantive part.
   §3.2: "When at least one usable 'secure' TLSA record is found, the SMTP client MUST use TLSA records to authenticate the SMTP server. Messages MUST NOT be delivered via the SMTP server if authentication fails."
   DaneFailurePolicy::Opportunistic permits falling back after a DANE failure. For SMTP that is a MUST NOT, not a configurable choice. DeliveryTarget::dane_records() already documents that its Some case is mandatory and that SmtpDaneConfig offers no setting permitting fallback -- so the state machine does not create the hole. What remains is making sure the entry point cannot route an SMTP delivery through a policy that would.
   Options: a distinct SMTP verify function that takes no failure policy at all, or a DaneFailurePolicy variant that cannot fall back. The first is probably right: an SMTP caller should not be offered the choice.

2. The async driver in pkix-dane-resolver: MX, A/AAAA and TLSA lookups feeding MxResolution::absorb. Mechanical now that the policy is settled -- mostly hickory wiring plus mapping Proof to DnssecStatus, which HickoryTlsaResolver::proof_to_status already does.

3. Placement of the entry point itself. The name checks and discovery both landed as feature-gated modules in pkix-dane, which argues for the entry point living in pkix-chain beside verify_tls_server_dane, with the async driver in pkix-dane-resolver.

## Not yet read

§2.1.2 (DNS error handling) and §2.1.3 (stub resolver considerations) in full, §6 (mandatory DANE), §8.1 (SNI support). §6 matters for piece C since SmtpDaneConfig::mandatory refers to it.

## Acceptance

[x] RFC 7672 usage-filtering requirement confirmed and recorded -- undefined/MAY, not MUST
[x] CN-ID decided: opt-in function on pkix-identity
[x] Reference identifier set per §3.2.2, matching per §3.2.3
[x] Placement decided for the name checks and discovery: feature-gated modules in pkix-dane
[x] §2.1 and §2.2 read before designing the MX lookup
[x] MX lookup DNSSEC-validated, with the status of both steps surfaced, honouring the MX-preference MUST and the A/AAAA-before-TLSA MUST
[ ] Reconcile §3.2's MUST-authenticate-once-available with DaneFailurePolicy
[ ] The async driver in pkix-dane-resolver
[ ] The entry point, and §6 read first
